source.title: Sequential Enumeration in Large Language Models
source.authors: Kuinan Hou; Marco Zorzi; Alberto Testolin

record.file_problem: The paper and supplementary material are present. Some figure labels and layouts are flattened or garbled in the extracted text.
record.tranche_reason: It compares downstream enumeration performance across model sizes, using accuracy and MAE rather than the held-out cross-entropy loss used in the scaling-law claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports an enumeration performance sweep across Llama model sizes. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit loss power laws, test extrapolation of loss, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Other task results, the coding condition, and latent-state analyses do not test the listed scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: It reports counting accuracy and MAE across Llama 3B, 8B and 70B, a downstream task outside the originals' setting. This bears on V6 only. There is no loss, no fit and no compute-optimal analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Within the Llama family, enumeration accuracy and MAE improve gradually with size from 3B to 70B, with no sharp emergence threshold. The authors also note that across models, size matters less than architecture or training. Their main conclusion is that no LLM counts spontaneously, and counting is reliable only when explicitly prompted and mainly in production tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Measures downstream enumeration accuracy and MAE across Llama sizes, rather than held-out cross-entropy loss; does not fit loss power laws or compute-optimal allocations.
record.code_released: Scripts and response files are said to be available in an anonymized drive; URL not stated.
record.problems: The size-scaling evidence is limited to three Llama sizes and a downstream enumeration task, not held-out loss. The reported endpoint values are approximate, and the text does not give per-size numerical values or uncertainty for the size sweep.
record.rows_left_out: Not applicable; the extracted rows cover the reported size-sweep accuracy and MAE. Other model comparisons and task conditions are not reported as the size-scaling result.

untested.parts: Any functional form or fit of task performance against scale, prediction of larger models' scores, a link to pretraining loss, and more than three sizes.

missing.what: Cross-family comparison: authors say smaller models (e.g. Qwen-32B) sometimes outperform larger ones, so size is less decisive than architecture or training. Supporting NAE values are in Table 1, e.g. Qwen mental 0.90 vs Llama-70B 1.03.
missing.locator: Section 4.1 last paragraph; Section 5 Discussion; Supplementary Table 1

missing.what: Per-size accuracy and MAE for Llama-8B (Figure 7 middle point), not given in the text.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V6: three model sizes, different Llama releases, pooled conditions, and a confound with invalid-trial rates. Absolute performance stays low (0.24 accuracy at 70B). Neither original source is involved.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from smaller-run loss fits.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests enumeration-task performance across sizes in one Llama family; it does not test other downstream tasks or relate task performance to pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, training setup, or curve shape.

rows.subject: Llama-3B, Llama-8B, Llama-70B (aggregate size sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Compared sequential-enumeration accuracy across increasing model sizes in the Llama family.

conditions.value: Llama; same architecture and training objective

rows.value: Increased from approximately 0.10 at 3B to 0.24 at 70B; reported to improve progressively across model sizes.
rows.note: The paper reports the trend for the size sweep as a whole; it does not provide text values for each size separately.
rows.check: The subjects are three separate releases (Llama-3.2-3B, 3.1-8B, 3.3-70B), so size is confounded with release and training differences, despite the paper's claim that only size differs. The values are pooled over tasks and prompting conditions. Invalid trials count as wrong, and valid-trial rates are lower for the small models (75.8% and 83.5% vs 93.3%), so format-following is confounded with size.

rows.subject: Llama-3B, Llama-8B, Llama-70B (aggregate size sweep)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean absolute error (MAE) in sequential enumeration across increasing model sizes in the Llama family.

conditions.value: Llama; same architecture and training objective

rows.value: Decreased from over 200 in the smallest model to around 70 in the largest; reported to improve progressively across model sizes.
rows.note: The paper reports the trend for the size sweep as a whole; it does not provide text values for each size separately.
rows.check: Same confounds as r1: the releases differ, values are pooled over conditions, and the invalid-trial rate differs by size. MAE is capped at 512, so values are approximate figure readings.

relationships.condition: Llama 3B/8B/70B instruct, sequential enumeration pooled over tasks and prompts
relationships.reason: Accuracy rises about 0.10 to 0.24 and MAE falls from over 200 to about 70, monotonically with size (r1, r2). This is only three points with no fit.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased monotonically from about 0.10 to 0.24 while MAE decreased from above 200 to about 70 across three sizes, without a fitted law.

relationships.condition: Across model families (Qwen-32B vs Llama-70B and others)
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not the rows: authors say size is less critical than architecture or training, and smaller models sometimes beat larger ones (Qwen-32B called remarkable). No row records this.
relationships.display_finding: Smaller models sometimes beat larger ones, with Qwen-32B performing strongly relative to Llama-70B and architecture or training judged more influential than size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
